title: Lead work teams on livestock farms

lessons.title: The role of a team leader on a livestock farm
lessons.html:
The role of a team leader on a livestock farm

As a team leader you are the link between the farm manager and the workers in the kraal, the dairy or the veld. You still do practical work, but you are also responsible for how well your team works together.

What a team leader does

  • Plans the day's work with the team: which camps to check, which animals to dip, who repairs the fence.
  • Gives clear instructions and checks that they are understood.
  • Makes sure people have the tools, protective clothing and transport they need.
  • Checks the quality of work and gives feedback.
  • Keeps simple records: attendance, tasks done, animals treated, problems found.
  • Reports problems to the manager quickly.

Leading by example

Workers watch what you do more than what you say. If you arrive on time, wear your gloves at the dip tank and handle animals calmly, your team will follow. If you take shortcuts, so will they.

Respect and fairness

Treat everyone the same, regardless of age, gender, language or where they come from. Do not have favourites. Many farm teams include people who have worked on the farm far longer than you; respect their experience and ask their advice. At the same time, you must apply the farm rules equally to everyone.

Knowing your limits

A team leader does not hire, fire or discipline on their own. You follow the farm's procedures and the law, such as the Basic Conditions of Employment Act and the Labour Relations Act. When there is a serious problem - a fight, theft, someone under the influence of alcohol, or a serious injury - stop the work if needed, keep people safe and call the manager.

lessons.title: Communication and giving instructions
lessons.html:
Communication and giving instructions

Clear instructions

A good instruction tells people what to do, where, when it must be finished, how it must be done safely, and who is responsible. For example: 'Sipho and Thabo, bring the heifers from camp 7 to the kraal by ten o'clock. Use the bakkie road, walk them slowly, and close every gate behind you.'

Check understanding

Ask the person to repeat the instruction in their own words. Use the language the team understands best. Show, do not only tell, especially for new tasks like using a dosing gun or reading an ear tag.

Toolbox talks

A short meeting of five to ten minutes at the start of the day is a good way to share the plan, remind people of safety risks for that task, and hear concerns. Topics might include: working with a bull in the kraal, handling dip chemicals, or what to do if a snake is seen.

Listening

Workers often notice problems first: a cow that is not eating, a leaking trough, a broken crush gate. Make it easy for them to tell you. Listen without interrupting, thank them, and act or explain what will happen.

Giving feedback

  • Praise good work specifically and in front of others.
  • Correct mistakes privately, calmly and soon after.
  • Focus on the work, not the person: 'The gate was left open' rather than 'You are careless.'
  • Agree what will be done differently next time.

Handling conflict

When two workers argue, separate them if needed, listen to each side alone, look for the facts, and help them agree a way forward. If it cannot be resolved, refer it to the manager.

lessons.title: Safety, motivation and team performance
lessons.html:
Safety, motivation and team performance

Safety is part of leadership

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, the employer must provide a safe workplace, and every worker must work safely and report hazards. As team leader you make sure this happens on the ground.

  • Check that protective clothing is used: gloves, overalls and boots at the dip, gloves for afterbirths, eye protection where labels require it.
  • Stop unsafe work - for example someone standing behind a kicking cow in the crush, or riding on the back of a moving bakkie.
  • Know where the first aid box is and who on the team has first aid training.
  • Report every injury and near miss.

Motivation

People work better when they understand why the job matters, are treated with respect, are trained, and see that good work is noticed. Explain how the team's work affects the farm: a properly dosed flock means fewer deaths and a healthy farm business that keeps jobs secure.

Training on the job

When a new worker joins, pair them with an experienced worker. Show the task, let them try under supervision, then check their work until they are competent. Record what training each person has had.

Measuring team performance

MeasureExample
Tasks completed on timeAll camps checked by midday
QualityEvery animal in the group dosed and recorded
SafetyNo injuries this month
AttendanceAbsence and lateness patterns

Key points

  • A team leader plans, instructs, checks and reports.
  • Lead by example and treat everyone fairly.
  • Give clear instructions and check understanding.
  • Praise in public, correct in private.
  • Stop unsafe work and report injuries and near misses.
